title: Kernel coexistence routing & KV-concurrency experiments
content:
Summary:

This is a working notes doc collating a set of experiments we ran to understand the tradeoffs when running TensorRT engines, Triton-hosted model instances, and a small custom CUDA kernel (fast-attn fusion) side-by-side on the same GPU pool. Focus is on routing heuristics, KV-cache concurrency, memory fragmentation, and the cost to switch execution modes.

Context / why this matters:
- Customers want the cost and latency benefits of TensorRT-optimized engines for common models, but we also need Triton for dynamic routing, ensemble logic, and model variants.
- A third path exists: custom CUDA kernels (we built a fused attention op) that can beat plain TRT in some short-context streaming workloads.
- Co-locating these execution modes on the same GPU introduces practical tradeoffs: memory layout fragmentation, CUDA context/stream contention, and model warmup penalties.

Goal:
- Produce a pragmatic set of heuristics and config flags to: 1) decide when to route to TRT vs Triton-hosted (pt/torchscript) vs custom-kernel path, 2) limit KV cache-induced stalls and memory OOMs, 3) reduce kernel-switch latency impact on tail p95.

Testbed (hardware + software):
- GPU: 4x A100 40GB per node (pinned tests on single GPU for microbenchmarks)
- Driver/CUDA: 525.60 / CUDA 12.1
- Triton: 23.01, configured with model control = explicit, instance_group: KIND_GPU single-instance for PT and TRT (separate models)
- TensorRT: 8.7 with INT8 calibration for one variant
- Custom kernel: fused-attn-v2 compiled into a cuModule, uses separate stream per request socket
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch kernel-coexistence-exp (see PR), scheduler: experimental preemptible-slicing v0.3
- Workloads: streaming chat (seq len 512 final tokens), short-turn chat (seq len <= 64), bursty batched embedding workloads (control case)

Experiment matrix run:
1) Baseline: all requests to Triton PT models (no TRT, no custom)
2) TRT-only: all requests to TensorRT engines
3) Mixed routing: short-turn -> custom-kernel, medium -> TRT, long -> Triton PT
4) Mixed with cache-sharing: KV cache shared across modes vs per-mode isolated caches
5) Warmup precompile on model load vs on-demand JIT/compile
6) Kernel-switch throttling: limit concurrent switches per GPU (0, 1, 4)

Metrics captured (per test):
- P50 / P95 / P99 latency (decode token level and request level)
- Throughput (tokens/sec and requests/sec)
- GPU utilization (SM%, memory%), GPU mem fragmentation (free blocks histogram)
- KV cache miss rate, cache eviction counts, average cache lookup latency
- Time spent in kernel-switch overhead (ms) measured by runtime hook
- Frequency and cost of Triton model instance spinup (ms)

Key observations (high level):
- TensorRT gives best raw throughput for medium-length sequences (seq 128-1024) when model fits comfortably in 40GB. P50 improved by ~25% vs Triton-PT, P95 improved by ~15% in isolation.
- The custom fused-attn kernel beats TRT on very short contexts (<64) for streaming workloads because it avoids certain TRT kernel launch overheads and does less memory copy for prefix KV handling.
- When mixing modes on the same GPU, memory fragmentation becomes the dominant failure mode: frequent TRT engine load/unload + custom kernel allocator patterns lead to OOMs even when aggregate RSS < device memory. Fragmentation increases with model churn (hot-swapping multiple TRT engines).
- KV cache sharing across modes reduces duplicate copies (good for memory), but increases contention on the cache metadata lock and raises p95 by ~10% for high-concurrency workloads. Isolated per-mode caches avoid lock contention but duplicate large KV buffers.
- Kernel-switch overhead (measured as time between last op of previous mode and first op of new mode executing on GPU stream) is non-trivial: median ~0.7ms, p99 ~12ms when there is interleaving of Triton instance spinup (streams/context changes). This directly affects tail latency for streaming token-by-token requests.

Micro-results (representative):
- Short-turn streaming (<=64): custom-kernel-only p50=18ms, p95=44ms. TRT p50=24ms p95=78ms. Triton-PT p50=30ms p95=110ms. Mixed routing (custom preferred) p95 tail increased to 92ms when cache is shared and concurrent switches >1 due to lock stall + kernel-switch spikes.
- Medium batch (seq 128-256): TRT throughput 1.3x Triton-PT, p95 15% lower. Custom kernel not competitive here.
- Cache sharing vs isolated: shared lowered memory footprint by ~30% on average but increased p95 by 8-12% under >50 concurrent requests.

Tradeoffs and heuristics we derived:
1) Routing heuristic (initial proposal):
   - If effective sequence length < 72 AND streaming token interval < 50ms -> route to custom-kernel path (fast path).
   - Else if model variant TRT has prebuilt engine and GPU free memory slack > reserved_swap_threshold -> route TRT.
   - Else route to Triton-PT.
   - Add rate-limited probing rule: try 1/200 requests to alternate path to measure regressions.

2) KV cache policy patterns:
   - Default: per-connection per-model-name cache (isolated). Avoids cross-mode locking on metadata.
   - Optional "shared-read-only" view: share large KV tensors read-only across modes but maintain per-mode metadata shims to avoid global locks. Implement via shared device pointer registry with lightweight atomic reference counting. (proto in PR linked).
   - Eviction policy: LRU + size hysteresis triggered earlier for mixed-mode nodes (lower watermark 65% instead of 85%) to prevent fragmentation OOM cascades.

3) Kernel-switch and warmup strategies:
   - Keep a small pool of warmed TRT engines and warmed custom kernels pinned to a GPU to reduce load/unload churn for high-traffic models (config: reserved_warm_slots per GPU).
   - Use CUDA graphs for steady-state decode loops when possible (we saw 2-3x p95 reduction for stable batched workloads). But graphs are brittle with dynamic lengths; only enable for variants with predictable seq-distribution.
   - Introduce a cost model for switch decisions: if estimated kernel-switch cost + expected tail impact > delta-latency-budget, prefer model fallbacks that avoid switching (e.g., route to Triton-PT instead of spinning up TRT engine for a single request).

Implementation notes / gotchas observed:
- Triton model instance spinup includes a device memory allocation wave that is not easily cooperatively reclaimed; this combined with TRT engine load order creates fragmentation hotspots. Ordering model loads by decreasing memory footprint helps but is not sufficient under churn.
- Custom kernels using cuMemPool reduced fragmentation significantly versus simple cudaMalloc/free for transient KV buffers. We should standardize mempool allocator for our custom ops.
- Using separate CUDA streams per request improved concurrency but increased the number of outstanding kernels and exacerbated kernel-switch overhead. A compromise is to multiplex lightweight requests on a shared decode stream with a per-request completion fence.
- Device pointer aliasing between Triton and our runtime (when sharing KV pointers) requires careful pinning semantics to avoid double-free on model unload; runtime hooks and a refcounted registry are necessary.

Unresolved questions / TODOs:
- How to surface cost model parameters to higher-level routing (host-level vs control-plane)? We need an API: estimated_switch_cost(gpu, mode_from, mode_to) which returns ms and memory delta. (TODO: instrument and export histogram metrics).
- Is there a viable middle ground to share KV without locks? The "shared-read-only" shim reduces lock contention in tests but adds complexity in correctness (concurrent eviction, refcounts). Need a safety spec.
- Should we force model pinning for high-traffic models (dedicated reserved slots) as a paid feature? Need pricing vs capacity analysis.
- Impact on multi-tenant isolation: fragmentation produced by one tenant can starve others — need tenant-aware memory isolation policies (cgroup-like on GPU).

Action items and next experiments:
- [Rafael] Flesh out and iterate the switch-cost API and add runtime histograms (SRV-1189).
- [Lina] Prototype shared-read-only KV shim with atomic reference counters and a unit test for concurrent eviction. (PR in progress).
- [Omar] Run a 72-hour production traffic replay with mixed routing enabled on a 4-node staging cluster to collect long-tail fragmentation stats.
- [Maya] Draft runtime config knobs: reserved_warm_slots, cache_mode: {isolated, shared-read-only}, kernel_switch_limit, switch_cost_threshold. Wire them into the console UI as experimental toggles.

Recommendations (practical defaults for initial rollout):
- Default to per-mode isolated KV caches and conservative routing that prefers TRT only when warmed engines already exist. This minimizes OOM and tail regressions for general customers.
- Enable custom-kernel path for customers with predominantly short-turn streaming workloads behind a feature flag and with pinned warm slots.
- Expose advanced memory policies (shared-read-only, lower eviction watermark) behind "optimized co-location" opt-in and require SLA guardrails.

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider an asynchronous engine loader that performs lazy allocation in a background worker with pre-allocated scratch pool to reduce fragmentation spikes.
- Explore ML-driven routing that uses real-time KPIs (cache hit, current free-block histogram) to decide on routing rather than static heuristics.

References and links:
- See PR with mempool and switch-cost hooks: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/4237
- Design doc for shared KV shim (draft): Confluence:ServingRuntime/KernelCoexistenceDraft
- Jira for extended staging run: SRV-1189

Appendix: measured histograms and raw traces (summaries)
- Attached artifacts in PR: microbenchmark traces per test (trt_vs_custom_2026-01-28.trace), gpu_free_block_hist_2026-01-30.csv
- Quick note: when concurrent switches > 4 on a single GPU, we observed p99 latency spikes correlated with free-block fragmentation events that required coalescing — this suggests we should throttle concurrent engine swaps aggressively.

End of draft - comments welcome.
